processes.description: The gas risk team keeps the price curves and location mappings used to value positions current. A round starts when a trader, a desk or a system change needs a curve added, a location remapped or a subregion code changed. Darron Giron, and later Kam Keiser, sets up the curve, asks the desk how it should be mapped, circulates the day's curve lists and official post IDs, and answers questions about curve moves. In the Netco transition, curve files were rebuilt, checked for retired curves and moved to a new directory before loading.
steps: A desk, trader or system change raises the need for a new curve, a remapping or a code change.
The risk analyst asks the desk how the location or deal set should be mapped.
The analyst sets up the curve following the written procedure and adds it to Tagg and the publication names.
The analyst records the official post ID and circulates the updated curve lists or mappings.
Desks check their regions for locations mapped to curves that will no longer be set and send back a list.
Questions about curve moves are answered with the traders' explanation of the market.

stalls.summary: Mapping decisions wait on the desk: the analyst cannot finish a curve or location set-up until someone says how it should be mapped, and some curve types depend on another group to set them up.
Newly set-up curves need a second hand-off before they are usable, being added to Tagg by someone else, and a reminder was needed to keep the routine post ID step from being skipped.
The Netco move forced curve files to be modified, relisted and relocated against a tight loading deadline, with lists of curves to load demanded at short notice.

contradictions.summary: Curve set-up is described both as something the risk analyst does directly and adds to Tagg, and as work certain curve types must leave to the global rate server group.

automation.approach: Keep one curve and location mapping register that a routine check compares with the official books: it flags locations mapped to retired curves, records the official post ID, and generates the circulated curve list, so the analyst only decides new mappings with the desk.
automation.rationale: The mail already shows a written procedure for setting up a curve and a macro that queries official books; a single SOP that joins set-up, mapping questions, post ID recording and list circulation would let any analyst run a round the same way, which mattered when the work moved from one person to another during Netco.

work_estimate.rationale: Most rounds are one curve set-up, a remapping or a post ID and curve list to circulate: looking up the mapping, entering the curve in the system and Tagg, and checking it took around 25 minutes. Netco rebuilds of whole curve files and region checks push the high end. Recording post IDs and building the list are mechanical; mapping choices stay with people.

processes.description: Heather Choate organises the annual customer trip and customer meeting. A round starts with a trip proposal or invitation sent to the business, then asks each desk to name the customers and employees it designates, sets deadlines for replacing guests who cannot attend, and finishes with a final guest list, activities and a rooming list sent for review. Reminders go out as the trip approaches.
steps: The organiser circulates the trip proposal for approval.
The invitation to the customer meeting is sent out.
Desks are asked to forward their customer and employee trip designations.
Replacements for declined guests are collected by a stated deadline.
The final guest list with activities and the rooming list are sent for review.
A reminder goes out as the trip approaches.

stalls.summary: The guest list depends on desks returning their designations and replacements, so the organiser has to set firm cut-off deadlines to close it.

automation.approach: A shared guest tracker holding designations, RSVPs, replacements, activities and room assignments, from which the final guest and rooming lists are produced directly, with a standard request message to desks carrying the cut-off date.
automation.rationale: Each round rebuilds the same lists from desk replies; one spreadsheet layout for designations, RSVPs and rooming removes the retyping and makes the final lists a by-product rather than a separate job.

work_estimate.rationale: The rounds show preparing a proposal or invitation, compiling designations and replacements, and building a final guest list with activities and a rooming list: around an hour of list building and checking per round, more for the proposal itself. A tracker template takes over compiling and formatting; choosing guests and arrangements stays with people.

processes.description: Desks need new trading books in Tagg, Sitara, TDS and RisktRAC when regions are split, new offices such as Chicago open, new counterparties arrive or the Netco books are created. Darron Giron gathers the book names, trader and portfolio details, fills in the book request form and sends it to the set-up team, which asks follow-up questions such as the trader's name and confirms when the book is set up. Lists of book and portfolio codes are circulated, and later Netco book creation and access requests were sent on in bulk.
steps: A desk change, new office or new counterparty creates the need for a book.
The risk analyst gathers book name, trader, portfolio and region and completes the book request form.
The request goes to the set-up team for each system: Tagg, Sitara, TDS or RisktRAC.
The set-up team asks for missing details such as the trader's name.
The analyst follows up on whether the books are complete.
Set-up is confirmed and the book and portfolio code lists are circulated for review.

stalls.summary: Requests go back and forth for missing details and completion status: the set-up team asks for trader names and the analyst has to ask whether requested books are done.
Confirmations of created Netco books reached someone who did not know why they were sent to him, and an analyst could not change the trading group himself.
Book lists are compiled by hand and admitted to be incomplete, leaving others to spot books that need fixing.

contradictions.summary: New book names were introduced in Tagg for the intramonth portfolios, while the desk questioned whether renaming books just to avoid confusion was necessary at all.

automation.approach: A single book request form that captures every required field up front (book name, trader, portfolio, region, systems) and routes to each system's set-up team, with a status list that shows when each book is live, replacing ad hoc requests and status questions.
automation.rationale: The follow-ups in the mail are about missing fields and unknown completion status; a complete request form with a status column addresses both and also serves as the circulated list of book codes.

work_estimate.rationale: A round means gathering book, trader and portfolio details, completing the request form and checking the books once created: around 20 minutes for one or a few books. Bulk Netco requests and full book code lists take longer. Form filling and status tracking are mechanical; deciding book structure is not.
